topics.name: Idioms & collocations
topics.note: These are fixed expressions where the words don't add up literally (a piece of cake, put up with, top-drawer). The only reliable approach is to meet them in context and memorise them whole.

topics.name: Vocabulary in context
topics.note: Choosing the word that fits the meaning and the collocations of the sentence. Watch the words just before and after the gap — they usually decide the answer.

topics.name: Prepositions & dependent prepositions
topics.note: Many verbs, adjectives and nouns take a fixed preposition: depend on, good at, interested in, afraid of, listen to, wait for, arrive at/in. These have to be learned as whole chunks.

topics.name: Gerund vs. infinitive
topics.note: Some verbs take -ing (enjoy, finish, avoid, mind, suggest, keep). Some take to + infinitive (want, decide, hope, promise, offer, agree). After prepositions always use -ing. A few (stop, remember, try) change meaning with each form.

topics.name: Mixed grammar
topics.note: A mix of points. Read the whole sentence, decide what is being tested (tense? preposition? word form?), then eliminate options that break that rule.

topics.name: Pronouns & possessives
topics.note: Subject (I, he, they) vs object (me, him, them) pronouns; possessive adjectives (my, his, their) come before a noun, possessive pronouns (mine, his, theirs) stand alone. Reflexives (myself, themselves) = subject and object are the same.

topics.name: The passive
topics.note: Passive = be (in the right tense) + past participle (is made, was built, has been sold, will be done). Use it when the doer is unknown, obvious or unimportant; add the doer with by if needed.

topics.name: Questions & word order
topics.note: Questions invert subject and auxiliary: (Wh-) + auxiliary + subject + verb (Where do you live? What has she done?). In reported or indirect questions the word order goes back to normal (I don't know where he lives).

topics.name: Phrasal verbs
topics.note: A verb + particle whose meaning is often idiomatic (give up, put off, look after, run out of). With many, an object pronoun goes in the middle (turn it on, not turn on it).

topics.name: Modal verbs
topics.note: Modals are followed by the bare infinitive. can/could ability & permission, must/have to obligation, mustn't prohibition vs don't have to = no obligation, should/ought to advice, might/may/could possibility. For deduction: must (sure it's true) / can't (sure it's false).

topics.name: Verb tenses & forms
topics.note: The options are forms of one verb, so the sentence is testing tense or form. Find the time reference (now / yesterday / since 2010 / tomorrow) and any signal words, then match the tense: -ing for continuous, have/has + participle for present perfect, will/going to for future.

topics.name: Easily confused words
topics.note: Pairs that learners mix up: make/do, say/tell, borrow/lend, bring/take, as/like, lie/lay, its/it's, been/gone. Check the exact pattern each one needs.

topics.name: Irregular verb forms
topics.note: Irregular verbs don't add -ed. Learn the three forms: base / past simple / past participle — go/went/gone, take/took/taken, break/broke/broken. The past participle is the one you need after have and in the passive.

topics.name: Present perfect vs. past simple
topics.note: Present perfect (have/has + past participle) links the past to now: experience (I've been to Japan), recent news, and unfinished time (this week, yet, already, since, for). Use past simple with a finished past time (yesterday, in 2019, ago).

topics.name: Comparatives & superlatives
topics.note: Short adjectives: -er / -est (cheap → cheaper → the cheapest). Longer adjectives: more / the most (expensive → more expensive). Use than after a comparative, and the before a superlative. Irregular: good → better → best; bad → worse → worst.

topics.name: Conditionals
topics.note: Zero: if + present, present (general truths). First: if + present, will + verb (real future possibility). Second: if + past, would + verb (unreal/unlikely present or future). Third: if + past perfect, would have + participle (unreal past).

topics.name: Relative clauses
topics.note: who for people, which for things, that for either (in defining clauses), whose for possession, where for places. You can drop the pronoun when it is the object of the clause (the film (that) I saw). Don't use what as a relative pronoun.

topics.name: Articles (a / an / the / zero)
topics.note: Use a/an with a singular countable noun mentioned for the first time (a before a consonant sound, an before a vowel sound). Use the when it is clear which one you mean, or it is unique. Use no article for plural or uncountable nouns in general (I like music), and most names.

topics.name: Question tags
topics.note: The tag reverses the main clause: positive statement → negative tag, and vice versa (You're coming, aren't you? / He didn't call, did he?). It repeats the auxiliary (or do/does/did), and uses a pronoun.

topics.name: Reported speech
topics.note: Tenses usually shift back one step (am → was, will → would, have done → had done), and pronouns / time words change (now → then, tomorrow → the next day). say has no person object; tell needs one (tell me).

topics.name: Quantifiers (some / any / much / many …)
topics.note: some in positives and offers/requests; any in negatives and questions. much + uncountable, many + plural countable (both mostly in negatives/questions); a lot of works everywhere. a few + countable, a little + uncountable = a small positive amount.

topics.name: Present simple vs. continuous
topics.note: Present simple for habits, routines and permanent facts (I work in a bank; water boils at 100°). Present continuous (am/is/are + -ing) for things happening now or around now, and fixed future arrangements (I'm working late today). Stative verbs (know, like, want, believe) are normally not continuous.

topics.name: Prepositions of time
topics.note: Use at for clock times, night, the weekend and festivals (at 6, at night, at Christmas). Use on for days and dates (on Monday, on 5 June, on my birthday). Use in for months, years, seasons and parts of the day (in July, in 2020, in winter, in the morning).

topics.name: Past simple vs. past continuous
topics.note: Past simple for finished actions and the main events of a story (she arrived, opened the door). Past continuous (was/were + -ing) for an action in progress around a past moment, often interrupted by a past simple action (while I was cooking, the phone rang).

topics.name: Talking about the future
topics.note: will for predictions, decisions made now and offers/promises. be going to for plans and intentions, and predictions from present evidence. Present continuous for fixed arrangements with a time/place. After when/if/before/as soon as, use the present, not will.

topics.name: Prepositions of place
topics.note: Use at for a point or a place seen as a point (at the door, at the bus stop, at school). Use in for enclosed or bounded spaces (in the room, in London, in a car). Use on for surfaces and lines (on the table, on the wall, on the bus).

topics.name: Verb 'to be' and there is / are
topics.note: Present: I am, he/she/it is, you/we/they are; negatives add not, questions invert (Is she…?). There is + singular / uncountable, there are + plural.

topics.name: used to / would (past habits)
topics.note: used to + infinitive for past habits and past states that are no longer true (I used to smoke; there used to be a shop here). Questions/negatives: did/didn't use to. be used to + -ing is different — it means 'be accustomed to'.
